q-333025.name: Question 1
q-333025.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t)\end{aligned}

q-333025.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{5t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/2ab8c69672acf64e93615960fdbb34445d4f81617cae16f90a8e4f30252607ba.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/d1b7ffd22ad77fe94a994659fb7a091692b23bafb3012a705e964419fb71e8aa.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
0<{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ is the dominant eigenvalue.

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/7a87773278ef8c921a9e7002a376bac1de99e969c2eb10e4a6f104a854094469.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/83885d091455a8f9b9a1c33556d9deeaee550d50dd665e016c2e8072c926f41a.png)
q-332486.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/e0446b7851fe0f0612d3db67de05188c0ed63af41ff1dfe2773158b2382fe722.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/ffa12152c9882d0953667f26e888d0fbac375f4cc0c348f3710799e1a6e22349.png)

q-333345.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=-2x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/6ea2d64a390187a28cfcd1c2692e97e5dc2ca5cb37649ba12cf71864e36958ea.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=2x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/2f2340cbff80765a5d3b551e87eb4207eebad05970e366ceeccd7bb142c0b677.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to $0.$

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is ${\lambda }_{1}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0.$

q-333503.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/97f7eb1fbddcd9d927447978efd4c42e705d6835bf0cc74525d42ded8c35346b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217341/assets/edc697ab38ae9a56d46181e0a45982b7045224de0cc3c4a786ddbc515f22196c.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>0.$

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form c1eλ1t[21]andc2eλ2t[−11].

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[21] has the equation y=12x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[21] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to v1=[−11] has the equation y=−x, as shown below.

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[−11] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector v1 as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is λ1.

Therefore, λ1>λ2>0.

q-333643.name: Question 5
q-333643.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[-1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[-1,\text{ }2]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options below regarding the given system.$\,$
$y=-x$ is {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
{{field-2}} is {{field-3}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-4}}.
q-333643.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-2x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-2x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

q-333637.name: Question 6
q-333637.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[-1,\text{ }1]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options below regarding the given system.$\,$
{{field-1}} is {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
$y=-x$ is {{field-3}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-4}}.
q-333637.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-x$ is $\text{a stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

q-333656.name: Question 9
q-333656.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=x(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[-1,\text{ }1]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options below regarding the given system.$\,$
$y=\frac{1}{2}x$ is {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
{{field-2}} is {{field-3}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-4}}.
q-333656.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=\frac{1}{2}x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

- The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x.
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, $y=-x$ is $\text{an unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$
